summary: This unit teaches you to choose, check and use the hand and power tools of a metalwork shop safely. You will learn to plan a small job, mark out and hold the work, and saw, snip, file, strike, punch and turn fasteners with the right hand tool. You will also learn to check and use portable power tools such as angle grinders and drills, corded or battery, and to clean, store and report on your tools.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It covers the **hand tools** and **portable power tools** that every welder and fabricator uses before and after welding: to measure and mark, cut, file, drill, bend, fit and take apart. Good welds start with parts that are cut square, filed clean and drilled in the right place.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. Most of the work is on mild steel flat bar, angle, tube and sheet, in the workshop and on small site jobs such as gates, grills and brackets.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan the job
Read the drawing or job sheet, list the steps in order and choose the right tool for each step.
Check tools before use
Spot loose hammer heads, split handles, mushroomed heads, blunt or broken blades, and damaged cables, plugs and guards; take faulty tools out of use.
Work safely
Wear the right PPE, keep the work area safe, control sparks, noise and dust, and protect the people around you.
Mark out and hold the work
Measure and mark from a true edge, and hold the work firmly in a vice or with clamps.
Use hand tools
Saw, snip, file, strike, punch and turn nuts and screws with the right hand tool and the right method.
Use power tools
Check, set up and use angle grinders, drills and other portable power tools, corded or battery, safely.
Finish and check the work
Remove burrs and check the sizes, squareness and holes against the drawing.
Care for tools and report
Clean, oil and store tools; tag and report damaged tools, faults and near misses.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, safety and PPE, checking tools, each hand tool, power tool safety, angle grinders, drills and tool care.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact names such as mallet, file card, TPI, centre punch, RCD) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: making a small steel bracket with hand tools (marking, sawing, filing, drilling, bending), and inspecting, using and storing portable power tools. The assessor watches how you work: checks, PPE, holding the work, and clean-up.

blocks.note: Learn the names of tools and their parts. Short-answer questions ask for exact words such as tang, safe edge, kerf, chuck key, spindle lock and double insulated.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Plan before you pick up a tool

flow: Read the drawing or job sheet: sizes, material, quantity and tolerance
List the steps in order, for example mark out, cut, file, drill, bend, deburr and check
Choose the right tool for each step
Get the material and check its size, type and condition
Check each tool and your PPE
Set up the work area and the vice or clamps
Ask your supervisor about anything unclear before you start

blocks.p: The **right tool** does the job safely, at the right speed, without damaging the work or itself. The wrong tool slips, breaks or spoils the job: a screwdriver used as a chisel, pliers used on a nut, or a file used as a lever all cause injuries.

head: Point
Hand tools
Power tools
rows: Examples
Hacksaw, snips, files, hammers, chisels, punches, screwdrivers, spanners, pliers
Angle grinder, drill, jigsaw, circular saw, cut-off saw
Speed and effort
Slow and tiring on big jobs
Fast, with much less effort
Control
Fine control for small, careful work
Even results on long cuts and many holes, but mistakes happen fast
Power needed
None: work anywhere, even in a power cut
Mains (110 V or 220 V) or a charged battery
Cost and upkeep
Cheap; little upkeep
Dearer; need checks, servicing and spare discs, bits and batteries
Main hazards
Cuts, stabs, slips, flying chips, strain
Electric shock, sparks and fire
Flying fragments, kickback
Noise, dust, vibration, entanglement

blocks.p: A good worker chooses for each step and often uses both: an angle grinder to cut a bar quickly, then a file to finish the end square.

blocks.note: Power cuts and sites with no supply are common. Keep hand tools sharp and battery packs charged, so the job can carry on. If a portable generator is used on site, a competent person sets it up, outdoors and away from doors and windows, because its exhaust gives off deadly carbon monoxide.
blocks.label: Jamaica

Check that
rows: Hammers
The head is tight on the handle and the wedge is in place
The handle is not split, cracked or loose
The face is not chipped or badly mushroomed

The head is not mushroomed or cracked
The edge or point is sharp and the right shape

A handle is fitted, tight and not split
The teeth are clean and not worn smooth
Hacksaw
The blade suits the job, its teeth point forward, and it is tight
The frame is not bent

The handle is not cracked; insulation on electrician's screwdrivers is undamaged

Measuring and marking tools
The rule's end is not worn or bent
The square is true
The scriber and punches are sharp

blocks.note: A damaged tool is never "made do" with. Do not tape a cracked handle or use a loose hammer head. Stop using it, label it DO NOT USE, put it apart from the good tools and tell your instructor or supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Safety, PPE and the work area

blocks.p: Most tool injuries come from a few hazards. Think about each one before you start, and choose how you will control it.

head: Hazard
Example
How you control it
rows: Cuts and stabs
Sharp edges and burrs, snips, scriber points, a slipping screwdriver
Deburr cut edges
Gloves when handling sheet and cut steel
Caps on points; cut away from your body
Flying particles
Chips from chiselling and punching, grinding sparks, a shattered disc
Safety glasses always; face shield over them for grinding
Guards in place
Screens to protect others
Sparks and fire
Grinding and cutting sparks landing on wood, rags, fuel or gas cylinders
Clear or cover anything that burns
Aim sparks away from people and fuel
Extinguisher at hand; check for smouldering afterwards
Electric shock
Damaged cables, wet conditions, the wrong supply
Check cables and plugs
Use an RCD or GFCI
Keep tools dry
Entanglement
Hair, sleeves, gloves or jewellery caught in a turning drill or grinder
Tie back long hair
Sleeves fastened; no rings, chains or lanyards
No loose gloves near a turning chuck or bit
Noise
Grinders, cut-off saws, hammering on steel
Ear muffs or plugs
Dust and fumes
Grinding painted or galvanised steel, cutting block or concrete
Extraction or good air flow
Dust mask or respirator as your instructor says
Vibration
Long spells with a grinder or hammer drill
Take breaks and share the work
Hold the tool firmly, not with a death grip
Report tingling or numb, white fingers
Strain and trips
Heavy bars, awkward lifts, cables across walkways
Lift with your legs; get help
Keep cables and offcuts out of walkways

head: PPE
Protects you from
When to wear it
rows: Safety glasses with side shields
Chips, filings, sparks and splinters
All the time in the workshop
Goggles
Dust and particles from every side
Dusty jobs, chiselling, overhead drilling
Face shield
Sparks and fragments hitting the whole face
Over safety glasses or goggles for grinding, wire brushing and cutting
Ear muffs or plugs
Noise that damages hearing for good
Grinding, cut-off saws, hammering, hammer drilling
Leather or cut-resistant gloves
Sharp edges, hot metal, sparks
Handling sheet and cut steel, grinding; not loose gloves near a turning drill bit
Dust mask or respirator
Fine dust and fumes
Sanding, cutting block or concrete, grinding painted or galvanised steel
Cotton or flame-resistant clothing
Sparks on the skin; synthetic cloth melts onto skin
Grinding and cutting, long sleeves fastened
Safety boots
Dropped steel and tools, sharp offcuts
All the time in the workshop and on site

blocks.note: Noise damage builds up slowly and does not heal. If you have to shout to be heard by someone about a metre or two away, the noise is loud enough to harm your hearing: wear hearing protection.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Setting up a safe work area

ul: Clear the area of rubbish, rags, cardboard and anything else that can burn before you grind or cut.
Plan where the sparks will go: down and away from people, doorways, gas cylinders, fuel, vehicles, wooden fences and dry grass.
Put up screens when grinding near other people, and warn people nearby before you start a noisy or sparking tool.
Keep a suitable fire extinguisher close by and know how to use it.
Run cables where nobody will trip over them, away from water, sharp edges and hot work.
Keep only the tools you need on the bench; put the rest away. Keep the floor dry and free of oil and offcuts.
Make sure there is enough light to see your marks.

blocks.note: In hot weather, sweat makes gloves slippery and lets electricity through the skin more easily. Keep a dry pair of gloves, dry your hands before you hold a power tool, drink water and take short breaks in the shade. Open-sided sheds and yards let the wind carry sparks: check where they will land.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Marking out and holding the work

blocks.p: Accurate work starts with accurate marks. You will learn marking out in depth in its own unit; here are the tools and habits you need for everyday jobs.

head: Tool
What it is for
Good practice
rows: Steel rule (often 300 mm)
Measuring and drawing straight lines, in millimetres
Stand it on its edge so the marks touch the work; look straight down at the mark
Tape measure
Longer lengths
Keep the hook clean and undamaged; do not let the blade snap back
Try square or engineer's square
Marking and checking lines and edges at 90°
Hold the stock firmly against a straight, clean edge
Scriber
Scratching a fine, sharp line on bright steel
Lean it so the point runs tight against the rule; keep a cap on it
Soapstone or metal marker
Marking dark or rusty steel, or steel to be flame cut or welded
Keep the line thin and sharpen the soapstone to a flat edge
Centre punch
Making a small dent so a drill bit starts in the right place
Put it exactly where two scribed lines cross; tap it once with a hammer
Odd-leg calipers and dividers
Lines parallel to an edge; circles and arcs
Set them against a rule's graduations

ul: Measure from a **true, square, clean end**. If the end of the bar is rough or out of square, square it first; otherwise every size you mark from it is wrong.
Measure twice and cut once. Check every mark against the drawing before you cut or drill.
Mark which side of the line is waste (for example with a cross) and cut on the waste side.
The **diameter** is the distance across a circle through its centre: a 10 mm drill bit makes a hole 10 mm across.

blocks.p: Work that moves can spoil the job and injure you. Before you saw, file, drill or grind, hold the work so it **cannot move, slip or vibrate**.

head: Holding device
Use
Good practice
rows: Bench vice (engineer's vice)
Holding work for sawing, filing, bending and light hammering
Hold the work low in the jaws, with the cut or filed edge close to them
Tighten by hand only: never hammer the handle or slide a pipe over it
Do not hammer hard on the jaws or slide: cast iron can crack
Soft jaws (aluminium, copper, fibre or plastic covers)
Protecting finished, polished or soft parts from the vice's teeth
Fit them over the vice jaws before you clamp the part
G-clamps and quick-release clamps
Clamping work to the bench or holding parts together
Pads clean; tighten firmly; check they will not get in the way of the tool
Locking pliers with flat or C-jaws
Holding small parts and holding parts together for tacking
Set the grip with the screw, then lock
Stands and trestles
Supporting long bars
Set at the height of the vice or bench so the bar does not lever the vice or tip over

blocks.note: Never hold small work in your hand to drill or grind it, and never stand or kneel on it. Clamp it, or hold it in the vice.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A hacksaw has a **frame**, a **blade**, a **handle** and a **wing nut** that tensions the blade. Most frames take 250 mm or 300 mm blades. The teeth are bent alternately left and right (the **set**), so the cut, called the **kerf**, is wider than the blade and the blade does not bind.

head: Teeth per inch (TPI)
Pitch
Typical use
rows: 14 TPI
Coarse
Soft metals and thick, solid sections
18 TPI
Medium
General work: mild steel bar and thicker angle
24 TPI
Fine
Thin angle, tube, conduit and thin bar
32 TPI
Very fine
Thin sheet and thin-walled tube

blocks.note: Choose the blade so that **at least three teeth** are always on the work. Too coarse a blade on thin metal lets a single tooth catch and snap off. Too fine a blade on thick, soft metal clogs and cuts slowly.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Loosen the wing nut and take out the old blade
Choose the blade for the material and thickness
Fit it with the teeth pointing forward, away from the handle, so it cuts on the push stroke
Tighten the wing nut until the blade is taut and does not twist; do not strain it
Check that the blade sits straight in the frame

ul: Mark the line all the way round the work with a scriber and square.
Hold the work firmly in the vice with the line close to the jaws, so it does not vibrate.
Start on the waste side of the line. A small nick made with the corner of a file, or your thumb beside the blade, guides the first strokes.
Start with light, short strokes, then use long, steady strokes using most of the blade's length.
Press on the forward stroke only and ease off on the return. Keep a steady rhythm, roughly 40 to 60 strokes a minute: sawing fast heats and blunts the teeth.
Keep the frame upright and watch the line on both sides of the work.
Slow down near the end of the cut and support the offcut so it does not fall or tear.
Remove the burrs from the cut ends.

head: Problem
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Blade snaps
Blade loose in the frame
Frame twisted or pressed sideways
Work loose in the vice
Too much pressure
Tension the blade, hold the work tight, keep the frame upright and let the teeth cut
Teeth strip off
Blade too coarse for thin metal
Cut started on a sharp corner
Finer blade; start on a flat face or a filed nick
Cut wanders off the line
Blade loose
Frame not upright
Not watching both sides
Tension the blade, square up and start a new cut if needed
Blade blunts quickly
Sawing too fast
Pressing on the return stroke
Very hard material
Slower, full strokes, pressure on the push only
New blade jams in an old cut
The old, worn blade had lost its set, so its cut is narrower than a new blade
Start a fresh cut beside the old one or from the other side

blocks.note: For thin-walled tube, use a fine blade and turn the tube in the vice as you cut, so the blade always works on the outer wall rather than sawing straight down through a thin side wall edge-on.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Tin snips** cut thin sheet like strong scissors. Straight snips cut straight lines and gentle curves. **Aviation (compound) snips** come as left-cut, right-cut and straight; the handle colour shows which, but colours vary by maker, so read the label.
Cut only sheet within the snips' rating, often about 1.2 mm mild steel for aviation snips; thicker sheet needs a guillotine, nibbler or grinder.
Wear gloves: snipped edges are razor sharp. Keep the waste on the side that curls away.
Never hammer the handles, use a pipe on them, or cut wire, nails or bar with snips: the blades chip.

head: Part of a file
What it is
rows: Tang
The pointed end that fits into the handle
Heel
The end of the blade next to the tang
Face
The flat, toothed surface
Edge and safe edge
The sides; a **safe edge** has no teeth, so you can file into a corner without cutting the side
Point
The far end of the blade
Handle
Wooden or plastic, often with a metal ring (ferrule); must always be fitted

blocks.p: Files are named by **length**, **shape** and **cut** (how coarse the teeth are). A longer file of the same cut has coarser teeth.

head: Cut (coarse to fine)
Use
rows: Rough
Very fast removal of soft metal
Bastard
Removing metal quickly from steel: the usual first file
Second cut
Bringing the work close to size with a finer finish
Smooth
Finishing to size with a smooth surface
Dead smooth
Very fine finishing

ul: **Single-cut** files have one set of parallel teeth and cut smoothly; **double-cut** files have two sets crossing and remove metal faster.
Shapes: **hand** (parallel width, one safe edge), **flat** (tapers to the point), **half-round**, **round**, **square**, **three-square** (triangular) and small **needle files** for fine work.
Hold the work low in the vice. Stand with your feet apart, one hand on the handle and the other near the point.
**Cross filing:** push the file forward across the work along its full length with even pressure. A file cuts only on the **forward stroke**, so ease off on the return.
Keep the file level; do not rock it, or the surface becomes rounded. Change direction now and then so you can see the high spots.
Check often with a try square against the light: when no light shows under the blade, the edge is square.
**Draw filing:** hold the file crosswise with both hands and push it along the length of the edge. It gives a smooth, flat finish along an edge.
**Pinning:** filings stuck in the teeth scratch the work. Clean the file with a **file card** (a stiff wire brush), and rub chalk on a smooth file to stop pinning.

blocks.note: Never use a file without a handle: the pointed tang can stab into your palm or wrist. Never use a file as a lever or hammer, or knock it on the vice to clean it: files are hard and brittle and snap.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Cutting and drilling leave a **burr**: a sharp, rough edge. **Deburring** means removing it with a file held at an angle, a deburring tool, or a countersink bit for holes. Deburr every edge: burrs cut hands, stop parts fitting, spoil measurements and stop paint covering the edge.

head: Hammer
Used for
rows: Ball pein (engineer's) hammer
General metalwork: striking punches and chisels, bending, riveting and peening. Sized by head weight, for example 0.45 kg.
Cross pein hammer
Starting small nails and pins; spreading metal
Claw hammer
Driving and pulling nails in timber
Club (lump) hammer
Heavy blows on cold chisels, bolsters and stakes
Sledge hammer
Very heavy blows, held in both hands, with everyone clear
Mallet (rubber, plastic, rawhide or wood)
Tapping parts into place or shaping sheet without marking it

ul: Hold the handle near its end and keep your eye on the target. Strike with the face square to the work: a glancing blow slips.
Choose a weight to suit the job: too light needs many blows; too heavy tires you and is hard to control.
**Never strike two hardened faces together**, such as hammer on hammer or a hammer on a file. Chips of hard steel fly off like bullets.
Never use a hammer with a loose head or a split handle.

blocks.h: Bending flat bar in the vice

flow: Mark the bend line all round the bar with a square and scriber
Grip the bar upright in the vice with the bend line exactly level with the top of the jaws
Push the bar over by hand to start the bend, then strike it close to the jaws with a ball pein hammer or mallet, using a block of wood or soft metal to spread the blows
Keep the blows square so the bar bends along the line and does not twist
Check the angle with a try square and correct it a little at a time

blocks.note: A bend uses up a little of the bar's length, so the legs come out slightly different from the flat sizes. The drawing or your instructor gives any bending allowance: mark from it, not from guesswork.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Tool
Used for
rows: Flat cold chisel
Cutting through rivets and bolts, chipping and splitting metal
Cross-cut chisel
Cutting narrow grooves
Centre punch
A dent so a drill bit starts in the right place
Pin punch
Driving out pins and rivets
Drift
Lining up holes in two parts
Letter and number punches
Stamping part numbers or job numbers

ul: Wear safety glasses, and use a screen so chips do not hit other people. Cut away from yourself.
Repeated blows spread the head into a **mushroom** whose cracked edges can break off and fly. Have it **dressed** (ground back to shape), or replace the tool.
Keep the cutting edge sharp; a blunt chisel needs heavy blows and slips.

head: Tip
Fits
Watch for
rows: Flat (slotted)
Straight slots
The tip must fill the slot's length and thickness
Phillips
Cross-head screws
Not the same as Pozidriv: the wrong one slips out (cams out)
Pozidriv
Cross-head screws with extra small lines between the arms
Use a Pozidriv tip
Torx (star) and hex
Star and hexagon recesses
Exact size only

ul: A tip **too small** slips and chews the screw head; a tip **too wide** damages the work around the screw.
Keep the shaft in line with the screw; push and turn at the same time.
Never hold small work in your palm while you turn a screw into it: if the tip slips, it goes into your hand.
Never use a screwdriver as a chisel, punch or lever.
Insulated screwdrivers for electrical work are marked with their voltage rating. Even so, never work on live parts unless you are trained and authorised.

head: Tool
Points to know
rows: Open-ended spanner
Quick to use; grips only two flats, so it can slip and spread on a tight nut
Ring spanner
Grips all round the nut; best for tight and rusty nuts
Combination spanner
Open end and ring end of the same size
Socket set with ratchet
Fast; reaches nuts in recesses; six-point sockets grip a tight nut best
Adjustable spanner
Fits many sizes but slips more. Close the jaws snugly on the flats and pull so the force is on the **fixed jaw**.
Hex (Allen) keys
Socket-head screws
Torque wrench
Tightens to the exact torque in the manual

ul: Use the **exact size**. Metric nuts are sized in millimetres across the flats (A/F); older and American nuts in inches. A 13 mm spanner on a ½ inch (12.7 mm) nut is slightly loose and rounds the corners.
**Pull** a spanner towards you. If you must push, push with the palm of an open hand, so your knuckles do not hit the steel when it slips.
Stand balanced, so you do not fall if the nut suddenly frees.
Never slide a pipe over a spanner for extra leverage, and never hit an ordinary spanner with a hammer: it can slip, snap or spread its jaws.

blocks.note: For a tight, rusty nut: wire-brush the thread, apply penetrating oil and give it time to soak in, then use a ring spanner or six-point socket of the right size. A few taps with a hammer on the nut's flats can help the oil in. Heat is used only by a competent person with permission. If it still will not move, ask your supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Tool
Used for
rows: Combination pliers
Gripping, bending and cutting wire
Long-nose pliers
Holding small parts and reaching into tight places
Side cutters (diagonal cutters)
Cutting wire close to a surface
Locking pliers
Clamping and holding parts firmly

ul: Do not use pliers on nuts and bolts: they slip and round off the corners.
When cutting wire, wear safety glasses and hold the short end so it does not fly off. Cut only soft wire within the tool's capacity, never hardened wire or steel bar.

sections.title: Power tool safety: supply, cables and checks

blocks.p: Portable power tools are **corded** (mains) or **cordless** (battery). Both can cut, burn or shock you in a moment, so they are checked before every use.

ul: JPS supplies **110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz**. Ordinary outlets are usually 110 V; some outlets in workshops are 220 V.

Read the tool's **rating plate**: voltage, frequency, power (watts) or current (amps), and speed (rpm). Plug a tool only into the supply it is made for. A 110–120 V tool plugged into 220 V will burn out and can catch fire.
Never force a plug into the wrong socket with an adapter, never cut off the ground (earth) pin, and do not overload outlets with multi-plugs.

blocks.h: How you are protected from shock

head: Protection
How it works
What you must do
rows: Grounded (earthed) tool
Its metal case is connected to the ground pin of its three-pin plug, so a fault trips the breaker instead of making the case live
Never remove the ground pin or use a lead without one
Double-insulated tool
Two layers of insulation, so no ground is needed. It carries the symbol of **a square inside a square** and usually has a two-pin plug.
Still check the cable and casing: cracked insulation defeats it
RCD or GFCI

A **residual current device** (called a GFCI, ground-fault circuit interrupter, on American-style equipment) senses current leaking to earth, perhaps through you, and cuts the power in a fraction of a second
Use one for all portable tools, especially outdoors or near water; press its TEST button before use: if it does not trip, do not use it
Fuse or circuit breaker
Protects the cable and circuit from overload and short circuit
It does not protect you from shock

flow: Inspection tag or label in date, if the Centre uses them
Cable: no cuts, burns, crushing, kinks, tape or coloured wires showing
Plug: not cracked; pins straight and tight; no burn marks; the cable's outer cover gripped where it enters
Casing: no cracks; screws in place; air vents clear
Switch: moves freely and turns the tool off; lock-on button not engaged
Guard and side handle fitted; disc, blade or bit the right type, undamaged and tight
Extension lead or reel checked the same way

ul: **Unplug the tool** (or take out the battery) before you change a disc, blade or bit, or adjust or clean it, so it cannot start by accident.
Make sure the switch is OFF before you plug in.
Carry a tool by its body, never by the cable, and pull out the plug, not the cable.
Use a lead rated for the tool's current, with sound plugs and sockets. Check it the same way as the tool.
**Unwind a cable reel fully** before use. A coiled cable cannot lose its heat, so it overheats and can melt; many reels show a lower rating for use when coiled.
Keep leads off wet ground and out of puddles, away from sharp edges and hot work, and out of walkways. Do not join several leads together.

blocks.note: Never use a power tool in the rain, on a wet floor or with wet hands. Water lets current pass through you to earth. Move the job under cover, or wait.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Sign
What to do
rows: Damaged cable or plug
Cracked casing
Tool hot, smoking or smelling of burning
A tingle or shock
Unusual noise or vibration
The RCD or breaker keeps tripping
Stop and switch off
Unplug it or remove the battery
Tag it DO NOT USE, with the fault, date and your name
Put it apart from the good tools
Report it to your supervisor
Do not try to repair it: electrical repairs are for a competent person

ul: A cordless tool is live whenever its battery is in. **Take the battery out** before changing a blade or bit, clearing a jam, cleaning or storing the tool.
Charge batteries only with the **maker's charger**, on a surface that will not burn, in a cool, ventilated place, and follow the Centre's rules about charging unattended.
Never use or charge a battery that is **swollen, cracked, leaking or very hot**. Move it away from anything that burns and report it: damaged lithium-ion batteries can catch fire.
Keep batteries out of direct sun and hot vehicles, and keep keys, coins and screws away from the terminals.

blocks.p: The angle grinder cuts, grinds and cleans steel. Common sizes take **115 mm or 125 mm** discs; big grinders take 180 mm or 230 mm discs. A small grinder's disc spins at around 10 000 to 12 000 rpm with no load (check the rating plate), so a disc that breaks throws pieces out like shrapnel.

head: Disc or accessory
Used for
Points to know
rows: Cutting disc (thin, flat)
Cutting bar, tube, angle and sheet
Cuts with its edge only. Never grind with its flat side: it is not made for side loads and can shatter.
Grinding disc (thick, depressed centre)
Removing metal, grinding welds and bevels
Held at a shallow angle to the work, as the maker says
Flap disc
Blending and finishing welds, removing rust and scale
Gives a smoother finish than a grinding disc
Wire cup or wheel brush
Removing rust, paint and slag
Loose wires fly out at high speed: face shield and glasses
Diamond blade
Cutting block, concrete and tile
Makes harmful dust: use water or extraction and a mask

head: Check
Why
rows: **Speed rating**: the maximum rpm on the disc is at least the grinder's rpm
A disc spun faster than its rating can burst
**Size and bore** match the grinder and its guard
Never fit a bigger disc than the tool is made for, or remove the guard to make one fit
**Type** suits the job and material (cutting or grinding; steel, stainless steel or masonry)
The wrong type wears fast, clogs or breaks
**Condition**: no cracks, chips, damp or swelling
A damaged disc can break up at speed
**Expiry (use-by) date**, often on the metal centre ring
Resin-bonded discs weaken with age; an out-of-date disc must not be used

flow: Unplug the grinder or take out its battery
Check the new disc: speed rating, size, type, condition and date
Fit the inner flange, then the disc the way the maker shows, then the outer nut
Press the spindle lock (only when the spindle is stopped) and tighten the nut with the disc key; never hammer it
Release the spindle lock and turn the disc by hand to check it runs free
Set the guard between the disc and you, and fit the side handle tightly
Stand to one side and run the grinder for a short time (many makers say about a minute), pointed away from people, to check it runs smoothly

ul: Clamp the work. Never hold it in one hand and the grinder in the other.
Hold the grinder firmly with **both hands**, using the side handle. Stand balanced, out of the line of the disc.
Let the disc reach full speed before it touches the work. Use light, steady pressure and let the disc do the work.
Keep a cutting disc straight in the cut; do not twist it.
Support the work so the cut **opens** as you go, with the offcut free to fall. If the cut closes, it pinches the disc and the grinder can **kick back** towards you.
Aim the sparks down and away from people and from anything that can burn; use screens.
When you finish, switch off and **let the disc stop** before you put the grinder down. Never stop a disc with your glove or the bench. Unplug it when you move away.
Never lock the switch on, and never remove the guard. If the grinder vibrates or the disc wobbles, stop and find out why.

blocks.note: **Kickback** happens when the disc is pinched or snags: the grinder jumps back at you with great force. Prevent it with the right support, a straight cut, both hands on the tool and your body out of the disc's line.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Drills are corded or battery. A **hammer drill** adds a hammering action for masonry; switch the hammer off for steel.
A **keyed chuck** is tightened with a chuck key: take the key out **every time** before switching on, or it is flung out. A **keyless chuck** is tightened by hand.
Larger drills have a side handle: use it, because a big bit that grabs can twist the drill and your wrist.

head: Drill bit
Material
rows: High-speed steel (HSS) twist bit
Mild steel and other metals; also wood and plastic
Cobalt HSS bit
Stainless steel and harder steels
Masonry bit (hard carbide tip)
Concrete, block and brick, with the hammer action on
Spade (flat) bit and wood bits
Timber
Hole saw
Large holes in sheet metal, timber and plastic
Step drill
Holes of several sizes in thin sheet and electrical boxes

flow: Read the drawing; scribe two lines that cross at the hole centre
Centre punch exactly where the lines cross
Clamp the work, with a piece of scrap wood underneath so you do not drill the bench
Fit a small pilot bit (for example 4 to 5 mm) tightly; remove the chuck key
Safety glasses on; sleeves and hair secured
Drill the pilot hole with the drill square to the work, steady pressure and a little cutting fluid
Open the hole to size with the larger bit at a slower speed
Ease off the pressure as the bit breaks through
Let the drill stop; brush away the swarf, deburr both sides and check the size and position

ul: **Speed:** small bits run faster; large bits, and harder metals, run slower. A bit that turns blue, smokes or gives blue chips is running too fast or too dry.
**Cutting fluid** cools the bit and helps it cut steel.
The bit is most likely to **grab at break-through**, when it can spin unclamped work round or wrench the drill. Ease off and hold firmly.
Swarf is sharp and hot: clear it with a brush, never your fingers. Do not wear loose gloves near a turning chuck.

head: Tool
Used for
Key safety points
rows: Jigsaw
Curved and straight cuts in sheet, timber and plastic
Blade to suit the material (fine teeth for metal)
Base plate flat on the work
Unplug or remove the battery to change the blade; let the blade stop before lifting it out
Hand-held circular saw
Straight cuts in timber and boards on site
The lower guard must spring back over the blade after the cut; never wedge or tie it open
Set the depth so the blade only just clears the work
Support the work so the cut does not close; two hands
Abrasive cut-off saw
Square cuts in bar, tube and angle
Work clamped in the saw's own vice
Guard in place; sparks aimed away from people
Let the disc stop before lifting the work out
Bench or pedestal grinder
Sharpening and dressing tools, light grinding
Tool rest set no more than about 3 mm from the wheel
Eye shields down and safety glasses on
Do not grind soft metals such as aluminium on it, or use the side of the wheel

blocks.p: Well-kept tools are safer, last longer, do better work and save time. Care for them every time you finish with them, not once a year.

head: Tools
Care
Storage
rows: Steel hand tools
Clean off dirt, filings and grease; wipe with a lightly oiled cloth
In a toolbox, drawer, rack or on a shadow board
Cutting tools: chisels, drill bits, scribers, snips
Keep sharp, or hand them to the person who sharpens them; dress mushroomed heads
Edges covered or in a holder so they do not chip or cut anyone
Files
Clean with a file card; keep dry and free of oil
Apart from each other so the teeth do not rub
Measuring tools
Wipe clean; check for damage
In a box or rack where they cannot be dropped or have heavy tools thrown on them
Power tools
Unplug or remove the battery; brush dust out of the vents; wipe clean; check for damage
Dry, in their case or on a shelf; cables coiled loosely, not wrapped tightly round the tool
Batteries and discs
Charge batteries with the maker's charger; keep discs dry
Discs flat, dry, in their packets and away from heavy objects

blocks.note: Damp, salty air rusts steel tools quickly, especially near the coast and in the rainy seasons. A thin film of light oil after use stops this. Do not leave tools in a damp tool bag overnight.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A **shadow board** has the outline of each tool painted where it hangs, so a missing tool shows at once.
Store heavy tools low and sharp tools with their edges covered.
Wrapping a cable tightly round a tool strains it where it enters the tool and breaks the wires inside: coil it in loose loops.

blocks.h: At the end of the job

flow: Switch off and unplug power tools, or take out the batteries
Let hot parts and discs cool
Check the finished work against the drawing
Clean and check each tool; report anything damaged
Return every tool to its proper place
Sweep up filings, offcuts and dust; sharp offcuts and scrap go in the scrap metal bin, rubbish in the right bin
Check the area for anything smouldering after grinding or cutting
Report to your supervisor: the job done, materials used, faults and near misses

head: Report
Examples
rows: Damaged or faulty tools
A split handle, a mushroomed chisel, a cut cable, a grinder that vibrates, a swollen battery
Injuries
Cuts, something in the eye, a burn or a shock, however small; first aid is given and it is written in the accident book
Near misses
A disc that shattered, a tingle from a drill, a spark that started a small fire
Missing tools and short materials
A tool not returned, discs or bits running out

blocks.note: Reporting is how faults are put right before someone is hurt. When you tag a faulty tool, write what is wrong, the date and your name, so the next person knows.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can read a drawing, plan the steps of a job and choose the right tool for each step.
I can compare hand tools and power tools and say when each is the better choice.
I can check hand tools before use and take a faulty tool out of use.
I can choose the right PPE for sawing, filing, drilling and grinding, and say what each item protects me from.
I can set up a safe work area and control sparks, noise, dust and trips.
I can measure and mark from a true edge and hold the work firmly in a vice or with clamps.
I can choose a hacksaw blade, fit it correctly and make a straight cut.
I can choose files by shape and cut, file an edge flat and square, draw file, and clean a file.
I can choose and use hammers, chisels, punches, screwdrivers, spanners and pliers correctly.
I can explain grounding, double insulation and RCDs, and check a power tool and extension lead before use.
I can use battery tools and charge their batteries safely.
I can check, fit and use a disc on an angle grinder safely, and explain kickback.
I can mark, punch and drill an accurate hole in steel with a portable drill.
I can deburr, clean up, store tools correctly and report faults and near misses.

terms: A coarse file cut used to remove metal quickly
The sharp, rough edge left after cutting or drilling
The part of a drill that grips the bit; a keyed chuck is tightened with a chuck key
Powered by a rechargeable battery instead of a mains cable
Removing burrs from cut or drilled edges
The distance across a circle through its centre
Built with two layers of insulation so no ground is needed; marked with a square inside a square
Pushing a file crosswise along an edge to give a smooth, flat finish
Grinding a mushroomed head or a worn edge back to its proper shape
A stiff wire brush for cleaning filings out of a file's teeth
The width of the cut made by a saw blade or disc
A sudden, violent jump of a grinder or saw back towards the user when the disc or blade is pinched
A hammer with a soft head of rubber, plastic, rawhide or wood
The spread, cracked head of a chisel or punch after many blows
A thin oil that creeps into rusted threads to help free them
A small hole drilled first to guide a larger bit
Filings stuck in a file's teeth, which scratch the work
Residual current device / ground-fault circuit interrupter: cuts the power fast if current leaks to earth
The edge of a file with no teeth
The way the teeth are bent left and right so the cut is wider than the blade
A board with tool outlines painted on it, showing where each tool goes
Covers of soft metal or fibre fitted over vice jaws to protect the work
A button that holds a grinder's spindle still while you change the disc
The chips and curls of metal made by drilling or cutting
The pointed end of a file that fits into the handle
Teeth per inch: how fine a saw blade is
A tool with two jaws, fixed to a bench, that holds work while you saw or file

c1.title: Handrail tube in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Tevin is a trainee at a small fabrication shop in Ocho Rios, St Ann. He is cutting 32 mm round tube with a 1.5 mm wall into posts for a guest house handrail, using a hacksaw. The blade already in the frame was fitted with its teeth pointing back towards the handle. Tevin saws fast, about two strokes a second, pressing hard both ways. Halfway through the third cut the blade snaps. He fits a new blade and pushes it straight into the half-finished cut.

c2.title: Hinge plates in Black River
c2.text: Shantelle works at a gate shop in Black River, St Elizabeth. She must take 2 mm off the end of each of six hinge plates cut from 50 × 6 mild steel flat bar, then drill two 12 mm holes in each. She starts filing with a smooth-cut file that has no handle. After a while, deep scratches appear on the filed ends and the file feels as if it is skating. For the holes she has a corded drill, a 5 mm and a 12 mm HSS bit, and a tin of cutting fluid.

c3.title: Cutting out a damaged gate bar in Linstead
c3.text: Oshane is sent to a customer's yard in Linstead, St Catherine, to cut out a bent bar from a steel gate and weld in a new one. He takes a 125 mm angle grinder rated 11 000 rpm. When he unpacks it, he sees that someone has taken the guard off. The cutting discs in the van are rated 12 250 rpm, but the date on their metal rings ran out last year. Dark clouds are building up over the hills.

c4.title: Start-of-shift tool check in Morant Bay
c4.text: At the start of a shift at a shop in Morant Bay, St Thomas, Keisha checks the power tools. The corded drill's rating plate reads 110–120 V, and the only free outlet near her bench is 220 V. A grinder carries a symbol of one square inside another and has a two-pin plug. When she presses the TEST button on the extension lead's GFCI, nothing happens. The battery pack of the cordless drill looks swollen.

c5.title: Seized nuts on a pump base in Santa Cruz
c5.text: Jermaine and his supervisor, Mr Lewis, are taking an old water pump off its steel base at a farm near Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. The four rusty nuts are ½ inch across the flats. Jermaine has a set of metric spanners and an adjustable spanner. He tries a 13 mm open-ended spanner, which slips, then reaches for a length of pipe to slide over the adjustable spanner. One nut's corners are already rounded.

questions.q: With the teeth pointing back towards the handle, how did Tevin's first blade cut?
o: It cut much faster, as the teeth bit harder on the pull
It cut on the pull stroke, so it cut poorly and blunted fast
It cut just the same, because hacksaw blades cut on both strokes
It cut only on thin tube and not on thick bar
questions.why: A hacksaw is designed to cut on the push stroke, with the teeth pointing forward, away from the handle. Fitted backwards, the teeth drag on the push and cut weakly on the pull, so the cut is slow and the teeth wear out.

questions.q: Apart from the backwards blade, what in Tevin's sawing is most likely to blunt and break his blades?
o: He is sawing too fast and pressing on the return stroke
The 1.5 mm tube wall is far too hard for any hacksaw blade
He holds the hacksaw handle with both of his hands
The handrail posts are being cut to the wrong length
questions.why: Fast strokes overheat the teeth and pressure on the return stroke wears them for no cutting. Long, steady strokes, roughly 40 to 60 a minute, with pressure on the push only, keep a blade sharp.

questions.q: The new blade jams as soon as Tevin pushes it into the half-finished cut. Why?
o: New blades always jam in a cut until their teeth have worn in
The tube has cooled and shrunk tight around the cut
The old cut is narrower, as the worn blade had lost its set
The new blade must have been fitted far too tightly in the frame
questions.why: The set of the teeth makes the kerf wider than the blade. A worn blade loses its set, so its cut is narrower, and a new blade binds in it. Start a fresh cut beside the old one or from the other side.

questions.q: How should Tevin cut the thin tube wall so the teeth do not snag?
o: Hold the tube loosely so that it can move with the blade
Turn the tube in the vice as he cuts, keeping a fine blade
Saw straight down through both walls without stopping at all
Use a coarse blade and press down hard on every stroke
questions.why: Sawing straight down puts a thin side wall edge-on to the blade, where few teeth touch and they catch. Turning the tube keeps the blade working on the outer wall, and a fine blade keeps several teeth on the metal.

questions.q: Shantelle must remove 2 mm and still get a smooth end. Which order of files is best?
o: Smooth cut first, then second cut, then bastard cut
Second cut only, as it is halfway between the others
Dead smooth cut only, pressing harder to go faster
Bastard cut first, then second cut, then smooth cut
questions.why: Start with a coarse file to remove metal quickly, then change to finer files to bring the end to size with a good finish. A smooth file alone is very slow at removing 2 mm of steel.

questions.q: What is causing the deep scratches on the filed ends?
o: The steel is too soft to take a smooth finish
She is pressing on the forward stroke only
Filings stuck in the file's teeth (pinning)
The file is too long for such short plates
questions.why: Pieces of metal lodged in the teeth stand proud and score the work, and the file skates. Clean it with a file card, and rub chalk on the file to stop the filings sticking.

questions.q: What is the main danger of filing with a file that has no handle?
o: The steel tang can stab into her palm or wrist
The file will cut on both strokes and wear out
The file will rust more quickly without a handle
The teeth will clog with filings much faster
questions.why: The tang is pointed. If the file catches or slips, the tang is driven into the hand. Fit a sound handle of the right size before using any file.

questions.q: Compared with the 5 mm pilot hole, how should Shantelle drill with the 12 mm bit?
o: At a higher speed, so it cuts through before it overheats
At the same speed but without the pilot hole being drilled
At top speed with no fluid, leaning her weight on the drill
At a slower speed, with steady pressure and cutting fluid
questions.why: Larger bits run slower, because their outer edge moves much faster than a small bit's at the same rpm. Steady pressure and cutting fluid keep the bit cool and cutting.

questions.q: At which moment is the 12 mm bit most likely to grab and spin the plate round?
o: As the bit first touches the centre punch mark
Halfway through, while the chips are curling off well
As the bit breaks through the far side of the plate
When the drill is switched off and slowing down
questions.why: At break-through the cutting edges can bite into the thin rim of metal left and grab. Clamp the work and ease off the pressure as the bit comes through.

questions.q: What should Oshane do about the missing guard?
o: Refit a guard that fits the grinder before using it at all
Use it for light cuts only, wearing a face shield
Use the grinder carefully, standing well back from the disc
Use it without a guard if the disc is new and in date
questions.why: The guard holds back pieces of a broken disc and keeps hands and clothing off it. A grinder must never be used without its guard, however careful the user is.

questions.q: The discs' speed rating is above the grinder's 11 000 rpm. Can Oshane use them?
o: Yes, because the speed rating is high enough
No, because the speed rating is too high
Yes, if he runs each one for longer first
No, because their use-by date has passed
questions.why: A speed rating at or above the grinder's rpm is right, but resin-bonded discs weaken with age and carry a use-by date. An out-of-date disc must not be used, whatever its speed rating.

questions.q: Oshane props the bar on two blocks, one on each side of his cut. Halfway through, the grinder jumps back at him. What caused it?
o: The bar sagged and closed on the disc, pinching it
The disc was spinning faster than its rating allows
The sparks heated the bar until it became soft
The work was too thin for a 125 mm grinder disc
questions.why: Supported on both sides, the bar sags in the middle and the cut closes on the disc, causing kickback. Support the work so the cut opens and the offcut can fall free, and keep both hands on the grinder.

questions.q: Rain starts to fall while Oshane is still cutting. What should he do?
o: Finish the cut quickly before the rain gets heavy
Stop, unplug, and move the work and tools under cover
Cover the grinder with a plastic bag and carry on
Wear rubber gloves so that the rain water cannot shock him
questions.why: Water lets current pass through the body to earth, and leads and outlets on wet ground are dangerous. Stop, make the tools safe and dry, and carry on only in dry conditions.

questions.q: What should Keisha do about the drill and the 220 V outlet?
o: Use it on 220 V for short jobs only
Use a plug adapter to fit the 220 V outlet
Plug it in, as 220 V will just make it faster
Find a 110 V outlet; never plug it into 220 V
questions.why: A tool rated 110–120 V will burn out, and can catch fire, on 220 V. Always match the tool's rating plate to the supply, and never force a plug into the wrong socket.

questions.q: What does the grinder's two-pin plug tell Keisha?
o: Someone has cut off its ground pin, so tag it
It is double insulated, so it needs no ground pin
It may only be plugged into a 220 V outlet in the shop
It must be used with a three-pin adapter
questions.why: The square-inside-a-square symbol means double insulated: two layers of insulation protect the user, so no ground pin is needed. A three-pin tool with its ground pin cut off is a different matter and must be tagged.

questions.q: The GFCI on the extension lead does not trip when Keisha presses TEST. What should she do?
o: Use it, as the button only checks the light
Use it indoors, where there is no water
Press the button harder until it trips
Take the lead out of use and report it
questions.why: The TEST button proves the device will cut the power if current leaks to earth. If it does not trip, it may not protect anyone, so the lead is tagged and reported.

questions.q: What is the safest action with the swollen battery pack?
o: Charge it fully so that it goes back to its shape
Use it until it runs flat, then throw it away
Stop using it, keep it from things that burn, report it
Tape round it tightly so that it fits back into the drill
questions.why: A swollen lithium-ion battery is damaged and can overheat and catch fire, especially on charge. Take it out of use, keep it away from combustibles and report it.

questions.q: Why did the 13 mm spanner slip on the ½ inch nuts?
o: ½ inch is 12.7 mm, so the spanner is slightly loose
Metric spanners are never strong enough for rust
Open-ended spanners cannot fit square nuts
½ inch is larger than 13 mm, so the spanner was too tight
questions.why: ½ inch is 12.7 mm. A 13 mm spanner is 0.3 mm too big, so it bears on the corners and slips, rounding them. Use the exact size, preferably a ring spanner or six-point socket.

questions.q: Mr Lewis stops Jermaine from using the pipe. What is the main danger?
o: The pipe will scratch the nuts and the pump base
The pipe makes the spanner turn the wrong way
The pipe stops penetrating oil getting to the thread
The extra force can snap the spanner or make it slip
questions.why: A pipe multiplies the force beyond what the spanner is made for. It can spread the jaws, snap the spanner or slip off, throwing the user onto the steel. Use penetrating oil, time and the right tool instead.

questions.q: Romario has been using an angle grinder for most of the day, and his fingers keep tingling and turning white. What should he do?
o: Grip the grinder much tighter to stop it shaking
Report it and take breaks from vibrating tools
Wear two pairs of gloves and carry on as before
Change to a bigger, heavier grinder for the rest
questions.why: Tingling, numb or white fingers are warning signs of damage from hand-arm vibration. Report them early; breaks, sharing the work and a firm but relaxed grip cut the exposure.
